paper.title: Machine Learning-Based Classification of Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus Using a Polygenic Risk Score and DNA Methylation.
paper.abstract:
Objectives: Type 2 diabetes mellitus (T2DM) arises from complex interactions between genetic and environmental factors, creating a need for approaches that integrate inherited susceptibility and cumulative environmental exposure. Previous models have focused on clinical or genetic data and provided limited mechanistic insight. This study developed a machine-learning model that integrated a polygenic risk score (PRS) and DNA methylation to classify prevalent T2DM and assessed their individual and combined contributions to classification performance.
Methods: Models were developed and validated using data from the Ansan/Ansung cohort (n = 1,318) and the independent Health Examinee cohort (n = 358). PRS was calculated using external genome-wide association study summary statistics, and DNA methylation features were represented by β-values at T2DM-related cytosine-phosphate-guanine sites. Three feature sets were compared: Base, Base + PRS, and Base + PRS + DNA methylation. Performance was evaluated using the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC). Decision curve analysis assessed clinical utility, and Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret the models.
Results: Adding PRS and then DNA methylation features progressively increased AUROC across algorithms. The linear support vector machine with the fully integrated feature set achieved the highest discrimination (AUROC = 0.896, AUPRC = 0.801). PRS improved accuracy, and DNA methylation data produced further gains, particularly in recall and F1-score. Decision curve analysis showed that the integrated model provided greater net benefit across clinically relevant threshold probabilities. SHAP analysis identified PRS as the most influential individual feature and DNA methylation features as the largest contributors at the group level.
Conclusions: Integrating PRS and DNA methylation improves the performance of machine-learning models for T2DM classification. Genetic and epigenetic factors thus provide complementary information for characterizing prevalent T2DM.

paper.title: Early prediction of clinical deterioration in older adults with suspected infection admitted from the emergency department to general wards: a multicenter machine learning study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Older adults with suspected infection admitted from the emergency department (ED) to general wards remain at considerable risk of early clinical deterioration. Conventional early warning scores may perform suboptimally in this population. We aimed to develop and externally validate machine learning models to predict early clinical deterioration within 48 h among older adults with suspected infection.
Methods: This multicenter retrospective study used electronic medical records from two tertiary medical centers for model development and internal validation between 2016 and 2023, with external validation using data from a regional hospital. Eligible patients were aged 65 years or older with clinically suspected infection. All records from the same patient were assigned to a single partition. Predictors included demographics, comorbidities, laboratory results, and vital signs recorded at emergency department triage and before ward transfer; missing data were handled using MissForest imputation with missingness indicators. Logistic regression (LR), random forest (RF), XGBoost, LightGBM, and CatBoost models were developed and compared with conventional early warning scores (NEWS, MEWS, mSOFA). The primary discrimination metric was the area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC), with the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC), calibration, decision-curve analysis, and Shapley Additive Explanations as secondary analyses.
Results: The development cohort comprised 96,871 ED visits, and the external validation cohort comprised 35,361 ED visits. CatBoost achieved the highest AUROC among all evaluated models (internal AUROC, 0.851; external AUROC, 0.829) and significantly outperformed the conventional early warning scores (external AUROC ≤ 0.70; all DeLong p < 0.001). For precision-recall performance (external event-rate baseline, 0.017), CatBoost achieved the highest external AUPRC (0.134), approximately eight times the baseline and more than three times the best conventional score, with the other machine-learning models ranging from 0.093 to 0.119. Calibration curves demonstrated good agreement between predicted and observed risks for the gradient-boosting models, whereas logistic regression showed greater deviation from the ideal diagonal.
Conclusions: Gradient boosting models, particularly CatBoost, achieved good discrimination for early clinical deterioration in older adults with suspected infection admitted from the ED to general wards, and outperformed conventional early warning scores. These models may support pre-ward-transfer risk assessment at the time of the ward-admission decision; prospective studies are warranted to confirm real-world effectiveness and guide clinical implementation.

paper.title: Dynamic machine learning for time-updated prediction of death within the next 24 hours in critically ill patients with acute myocardial infarction.
paper.abstract: Critically ill patients with acute myocardial infarction (AMI) admitted to the intensive care unit (ICU) may deteriorate rapidly, yet most existing prognostic tools rely on static admission information and do not update risk as clinical status evolves. We developed and externally validated a dynamic landmark-based machine-learning model to predict in-hospital death within the next 24 hours during ICU stay. Adult ICU stays with AMI were identified in eICU-CRD for model development and internal validation and in MIMIC-IV for external validation. Repeated 6-hour landmarks were generated, and a dynamic LightGBM model was compared with dynamic penalized logistic regression, static first-window LightGBM, dynamic SOFA, an AMI nomogram, APS III/APACHE III, and OASIS. Internal validation included 109,675 eligible landmarks from 10,613 ICU stays; external validation included 52,946 landmarks from 4,505 ICU stays. Dynamic LightGBM achieved the best internal performance (AUROC 0.892, AUPRC 0.231, Brier score 0.0142) and remained the strongest model externally (AUROC 0.868, AUPRC 0.215, Brier score 0.0182). External recalibration improved calibration while preserving discrimination. Decision-curve analysis showed the highest net benefit across clinically relevant thresholds, and the model provided earlier warning with the lowest alert burden (28.4 alerts per 100 patient-days). Performance remained stable across prespecified high-acuity subgroups and sensitivity analyses. These findings support dynamic landmark-based machine learning as a practical framework for short-term mortality monitoring in critically ill patients with AMI.

paper.title: Real-time structuring of the clinical information section for dopamine transporter SPECT reporting with a small language model pipeline: development and external validation.
paper.abstract:
Background: Accurate interpretation of dopamine transporter (DAT)-SPECT depends on clinical context, including symptoms, medication, comorbidities, and structural imaging findings. In routine practice, however, this information is often documented as heterogeneous free text, which may hinder consistent consideration of clinically relevant parameters and limit guideline-compliant reporting. We therefore developed and evaluated a locally deployable small language model (SLM)-based pipeline to structure and standardize the clinical information section for DAT-SPECT reporting. Two retrospective datasets were used. The in-house dataset included clinical information sections from 2,990 DAT-SPECT examinations and was split into training (n = 2,700) and internal test data (n = 290). The external validation dataset comprised 595 clinical information sections from a second institution. A structured dictionary (466 entries across 12 categories) was created by two experienced DAT-SPECT readers and used to manually annotate the training and internal test samples. A Qwen3 1.7B model was fine-tuned by supervised learning to reproduce expert annotations. A rule-based postprocessing pipeline converted model outputs into report-ready structured text, including removal of redundant entries, automated suggestion of scan indication, consolidation of symptom lateralization and time course, reminders for missing guideline-relevant elements, and medication interaction checks. Internal test performance was assessed by expert comparison of SLM output with manual annotation. External performance was assessed by counting the manual corrections required in the postprocessed output under strict criteria.
Results: In the internal test dataset, the postprocessed SLM output provided the same information as the expert annotation in 196/290 cases (67.6%), including exact matches in 147/290 (50.7%). Interpretation differences due to free-text ambiguity occurred in 13/290 cases (4.5%), and SLM errors in 41/290 cases (14.1%). In 40/290 cases (13.8%), the SLM output was judged superior to the manual annotation. Among the error cases, 36/41 (87.8%) involved only a single erroneous or missing item. In the external dataset, 446/595 postprocessed outputs (75.0%) required no manual correction before inclusion in the report. Among the remaining 149/595 cases (25.0%), correction of only a single item was required in 111 cases (18.7% of all cases). The mean number of corrections was 0.34 items per case, corresponding to 6.0% of all structured items.
Conclusions: A locally deployable SLM combined with rule-based postprocessing can transform free-text clinical information for DAT-SPECT into standardized, report-ready documentation with good practical usability in an external dataset. End-to-end processing times of typically less than one second on the tested hardware support the feasibility of real-time local deployment. Prospective studies are required to determine its effects on clinical workflow and reporting quality.

paper.title: Multicenter external validation of CT-based deep learning for proximal femoral fracture classification and quantitative fracture-line assessment.
paper.abstract:
Objective: To develop and externally validate a CT-based deep learning CAD system for proximal femoral fracture classification and fracture-line angle quantification and to preliminarily evaluate its clinical utility in a reader study.
Materials And Methods: In this multicenter retrospective study, coronal CT images from four institutions were used for training (259 patients, 19,844 annotated images) and internal validation (91 patients, 92 hips). External validation included 200 patients from independent institutions scanned with CT systems from two vendors. A ResNet-50-based convolutional neural network was used to perform fracture region segmentation, fracture classification, pelvic fracture detection, and fracture line angle estimation. The diagnostic performance and fracture-line angle agreement were evaluated using internal and external validation datasets. An exploratory reader study involving six readers was conducted to assess the effects of CAD assistance.
Results: Overall classification accuracy was 95.7% (κ = 0.944) internally and 91.5% (κ = 0.887) externally; F1-score ranges were 0.927-0.982 and 0.667-0.952, respectively. The fracture-line angle mean absolute errors were 4.54° and 6.26°, approaching the interobserver errors between orthopedic specialists (3.64° and 5.18°), with corresponding ICCs of 0.817 and 0.736, respectively. In the exploratory reader study, residents showed higher sensitivity with CAD assistance for non-displaced femoral neck fractures (0.78 vs. 0.47), with high specificity.
Conclusion: This multicenter CT-based CAD system demonstrated accurate and generalizable fracture region segmentation, proximal femoral fracture classification, and objective fracture line angle quantification across independent datasets. The proposed approach has the potential to support diagnosis and preoperative assessment of proximal femoral fractures.

paper.title: Prognostic marker related to nicotinamide metabolism in ovarian cancer based on multiple machine learning approaches.
paper.abstract:
Background: Nicotinamide metabolism plays a critical role in the formation and progression of ovarian cancer (OC). This study aimed to develop a prognostic marker for OC, focusing specifically on nicotinamide metabolism pathways, using multiple machine learning approaches.
Methods: Gene expression data from TCGA training cohort (n = 427) and two independent validation cohorts: GSE19829 (n = 28) and ICGC-OV (n = 112), were analyzed. A consensus prognostic model was constructed from a combination of 112 machine learning algorithms. Protein-protein interaction networks, survival analysis, gene set enrichment, mutation profiling, and immune infiltration assessments were performed. Single-cell data from GSE147082 (n = 6)were used for quality control, cell annotation, and developmental trajectory analysis.
Results: Our results identify stable prognostic genes associated with OC and developed a risk scoring system that effectively stratifies patients into high- and low-risk groups with significant survival differences (p < 0.05). A final prognostic model base on 23 hub genes demonstrated a robust mean concordance index (C-index) of 0.709. Furthermore, we reveal significant disparities in immune checkpoint markers expression between different risk groups, underscoring potential therapeutic implications. Finally, the model is tested on additional cancer types and clinical utility is assessed using calibration and decision curve analysis.
Conclusions: This multiple machine learning tool develops a prognostic marker related to Nicotinamide metabolism for individuals with OC and could potentially be applied to other cancers in the future.

paper.title: A reproducible structural brain axis of alcohol use severity.
paper.abstract: Alcohol use is linked to distributed structural brain alterations, but population-level alcohol-related neurobiology remains difficult to quantify. We tested whether deep learning-derived MRI representations capture reproducible variation in alcohol consumption severity and converge with clinical and biological markers. Representations were extracted from gray-matter volume maps in the German National Cohort (NAKO; N ≈ 28,000). Ridge-regression scores were derived from structural MRI to estimate alcohol consumption severity, measured with the Alcohol Use Disorders Identification Test-Consumption (AUDIT-C). Models were trained in NAKO, externally validated in UK Biobank (N ≈ 25,000), evaluated in FOR2107 (N ≈ 1900), and tested against ICD-10 alcohol use disorder (AUD), alcohol-related biomarkers, and cognition. In NAKO, the structural MRI-derived ridge-regression score correlated with measured AUDIT-C severity (r = 0.11; 95% CI, 0.09-0.12; qFDR = 1.2 × 10-70; MAE = 1.64). This association replicated in UK Biobank (r = 0.09; 95% CI, 0.07-0.10; qFDR = 4.9 × 10-41; MAE = 1.96) and generalized to AUD, with higher odds in the highest versus lowest brain-score quintile (OR = 2.28; 95% CI, 1.49-3.48; qFDR = 3.9 × 10-4). The score was associated with gamma-glutamyl transferase (β = 1.17 U/L; qFDR = 0.007), mean corpuscular volume (β = 14.26 fL; qFDR = 4.4 × 10-4), and slower reaction time (β = 163.40 ms; qFDR = 3.0 × 10-5). Deep learning-derived structural MRI representations capture weak but reproducible alcohol-related brain variation that converges with AUD diagnosis, peripheral biomarkers, and cognition, supporting their use in population-level addiction neuroscience while underscoring limits for individual-level prediction.

paper.title: Multimodal multitask deep learning for predicting tertiary lymphoid structures and peritoneal recurrence in gastric cancer: a multicentre development, validation, and testing study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Peritoneal recurrence remains a common and fatal complication following curative gastric cancer surgery. Tertiary lymphoid structures are crucial indicators of immune response in cancer, and their maturation is associated with better prognosis and therapy outcomes. Evaluation of these structures could improve patient stratification for treatment of cancer but is hindered by the invasive and biased nature of histological methods. This study aimed to explore a non-invasive radiological method of assessment in patients with gastric cancer, using a novel multitask hybrid model to predict the presence and maturation status of tertiary lymphoid structures and peritoneal recurrence-free survival.
Methods: We developed CTransNet, a multitask hybrid model combining a convolutional neural network (ResNet50) and a Transformer model to predict tertiary lymphoid structure maturation and peritoneal recurrence-free survival in patients with gastric cancer. The study used retrospective data from eight Chinese cohorts of patients treated for gastric cancer at Nanfang Hospital, Sun Yat-sen University Cancer Center, Yunnan Cancer Hospital, and Guangdong Provincial Hospital of Chinese Medicine (one training cohort, two internal validation cohorts, three external validation cohorts, and two independent cohorts of patients treated with anti-PD-1 or anti-PD-L1 inhibitors for at least two cycles). Patients were classified into three categories based on the presence and maturation of tertiary lymphoid structures (identified using haematoxylin-eosin and immunohistochemistry staining): TLS0 (absent tertiary lymphoid structures), TLS1 (primary follicle-like tertiary lymphoid structures without germinal centres), and TLS2 (secondary follicle-like tertiary lymphoid structures with germinal centres [ie, more mature structures]). Peritoneal recurrence was assessed using imaging (ultrasonography, CT, or PET-CT), clinical signs, or reoperation. We evaluated the accuracy of the multitask hybrid model in classifying patient-level tertiary lymphoid structure status using receiver operating characteristic analysis. Patients were stratified into risk groups using the median predicted score from the training cohort (high vs low), which was then applied to the validation cohorts. Survival outcomes (peritoneal recurrence-free survival, disease-free survival, and overall survival) were analysed using Kaplan-Meier methods and Cox proportional hazards models. We also analysed the relationships between predicted scores and responses to chemotherapy and immunotherapy.
Findings: Patients in the Chinese cohorts were recruited between Jan 1, 2005, and Feb 28, 2022. In the training cohort, for classifying patient-level tertiary lymphoid structure status, values for area under the receiver operating characteristic curve were 0·910 (95% CI 0·882-0·938) for TLS0, 0·925 (0·899-0·951) for TLS1, and 0·953 (0·933-0·974) for TLS2. For predicting peritoneal recurrence-free survival, the model achieved a concordance index of 0·654 (95% CI 0·620-0·688) in the training cohort. Across all cohorts, patients with low model scores had substantially higher 5-year peritoneal recurrence rates than those with high scores (eg, 66·69%, 95% CI 60·11-73·27 vs 26·28%, 20·05-32·51; p<0·0001 in the training cohort). Multivariate analysis confirmed risk stratification based on the multitask hybrid model score as an independent predictor of peritoneal recurrence-free survival, disease-free survival, and overall survival. Analysis of patients with stage II or stage III disease in the training cohort and internal and external validation cohorts showed that in those with low predicted scores versus high predicted scores, adjuvant chemotherapy was associated with improved disease-free survival and overall survival in patients with low scores but not those with high scores. In the immunotherapy cohorts, objective response rates were higher for patients with high predicted scores than for those with low predicted scores (54·5% vs 5·6%; p<0·0001 in immunotherapy cohort 1 and 53·1% vs 9·7%; p=0·0010 in immunotherapy cohort 2).
Interpretation: By accurately predicting tertiary lymphoid structure status, peritoneal recurrence, and survival, the multitask hybrid model shows strong potential as a non-invasive tool for personalised gastric cancer care. The model's potential to identify patients who might benefit from adjuvant chemotherapy and are more likely to respond to immunotherapy could help clinicians to optimise treatment strategies.
Funding: None.

paper.title: Machine learning explainability of acute toxicity in salvage prostate cancer radiotherapy: A multicentric investigation.
paper.abstract:
Background And Purpose: To develop and validate an explainable machine learning (ML) model for early prediction of grade ≥ 2 acute gastrointestinal (GI) and genitourinary (GU) toxicities in prostate cancer patients treated with salvage radiotherapy (SRT) post-prostatectomy.
Material And Methods: Patient-, surgical- and treatment-related data from 454 patients treated with SRT in three Italian centers were collected and analyzed. 271 patients from two centers served as the training and internal validation set, while 183 patients from the third institution were used as the external test set. The light gradient boosting machine (LGBM) algorithm was used to construct the models. The SHapley Additive exPlanation (SHAP) method was used to rank the feature importance and explain the final model.
Results: The rates of grade ≥ 2 GI and GU toxicities were 28.2% and 21.8%, respectively. The LGBM model accurately predicted the risk of GI and GU acute toxicity in both the internal validation (GI: AUC = 0.784, GU: AUC = 0.911) and the external test set (GI: AUC = 0.706, GU: AUC = 0.855). The calibration curve showed high agreement between the predicted and observed risks. The most significant determinants of both acute toxicities were the surgical technique, the CTV to PTV margin, the type of androgen deprivation therapy, the extent of lymphadenectomy and the dose fractionation.
Conclusion: This study underscores the importance of integrating patient-, surgical-, and radiotherapy-specific factors in predictive models to minimize adverse effects. The LGBM algorithm provides a robust framework to identify high-risk patients early and provides a basis for individualized patient treatment plans.

paper.title: Machine learning-based prediction of hungry bone syndrome in secondary hyperparathyroidism: A multicenter study integrating clinical and bone turnover markers.
paper.abstract:
Objective: Hungry bone syndrome (HBS) is characterized by hypocalcemia following parathyroidectomy for secondary hyperparathyroidism (SHPT). Current prediction tools are limited by single-center designs and often lack bone turnover markers. We aimed to develop and validate a machine learning model for HBS risk prediction.
Methods: This multicenter study included 992 patients from two tertiary hospitals, with 718 used for training and internal testing and 274 for independent external validation. Predictors were selected from the intersection of four feature selection algorithms. Seven machine learning algorithms were trained using fivefold cross-validation and evaluated using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Shapley Additive Explanations (SHAP) were used to interpret the optimal model.
Results: Predictors comprised alkaline phosphatase (ALP), procollagen type I N-terminal propeptide (PINP), C-terminal cross-linked telopeptide of type I collagen (CTX), serum calcium, and parathyroid hormone (PTH). Extreme gradient boosting (XGB) achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.821 (95% CI 0.756, 0.887) in internal testing. The external validation AUC was 0.813 (95% CI 0.762, 0.864). The positive predictive value (PPV) and negative predictive value (NPV) were 0.843 and 0.683 in the internal test set and 0.795 and 0.634 in the external validation set, respectively. SHAP analysis associated higher ALP, PTH, CTX, and PINP levels with increased HBS risk and higher serum calcium with lower risk. The model was deployed as a publicly accessible web-based calculator.
Conclusions: We constructed an interpretable XGB model with good discrimination for predicting HBS in patients with SHPT by integrating specific bone turnover markers with routine clinical variables. This web-based tool facilitates early risk stratification and may support personalized perioperative management, although the residual risk among patients classified as low risk suggests that it should complement rather than replace clinical assessment.

paper.title: Comprehensive Clinical Decision-Support Framework for Obesity Prevention Using Large-Scale Health Checkup Data: Development and Evaluation Study.
paper.abstract:
Background: Obesity prevention requires identifying nonobese adults at risk of developing obesity. Routine health checkups collect anthropometric, laboratory, medical history, and lifestyle information, but screening primarily describes current anthropometric status and does not directly provide individualized estimates of future risk for preventive counseling.
Objective: This study aimed to develop and evaluate a comprehensive clinical decision-support framework for obesity prevention using large-scale health checkup data.
Methods: This retrospective cohort study used repeated examination data from the Kangbuk Samsung Health Study. Adults with BMI less than 25 kg/m², at least 3 health checkup visits, a 2-year obesity-free washout period, and postindex follow-up were included. Incident obesity was defined as the first follow-up BMI of 25 kg/m² or higher. The framework integrated a single-visit prediction tier (which we termed lite), a survival component for time-to-transition context, a repeated-measurement updating tier (which we termed plus), and an explainability layer. The primary lite-tier and survival analyses used training-set-only imputation. A previously exported lite-tier Extreme Gradient Boosting (XGBoost) component was externally evaluated in 328,268 National Health Insurance Service (NHIS) participants.
Results: Among 231,683 initially nonobese participants, 38,094 developed incident obesity. In the aligned 5-year visit-1 test cohort, 4088 of 21,783 (18.8%) participants developed obesity. The lite-tier ensemble achieved an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) of 0.918, an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.693, a Brier score of 0.087, and an expected calibration error of 0.005. AUPRC was approximately 3.7 times the no-information reference. AUROCs were 0.913 for BMI-only and 0.914 for BMI+age+sex. Observed 5-year incidence ranged from 0.1% (6/4357) to 64.7% (2821/4357) across accelerated failure time (AFT) risk quintiles. The plus tier achieved a landmark-row AUROC of 0.899 with less favorable calibration. The previously exported lite-tier XGBoost component achieved an external AUROC of 0.857, AUPRC of 0.575, and Brier score of 0.132.
Conclusions: Large-scale health checkup data supported an integrated framework for single-visit triage, temporal risk context, risk-domain explanation, and exploratory repeated-measurement updating, providing a basis for prevention-oriented risk communication and follow-up prioritization. The overall gain in discrimination beyond BMI was modest, and the effects on clinical decisions and obesity prevention require prospective evaluation.

paper.title: A Multi-Model Framework for Explainable Sepsis Mortality Prediction With Dynamic Fairness and Drift Analysis.
paper.abstract: Artificial intelligence-based clinical decision support systems can materially improve risk prediction and resource allocation in critical care, yet their sustained governance raises an underexamined problem for the health informatics community: model fairness and interpretability are typically certified once, at deployment, even though both properties evolve as models are periodically retrained within feedback-laden sociotechnical environments. This study reframes algorithmic fairness as a dynamic, lifecycle property rather than a static deployment checkpoint, and develops a multi-model framework that jointly addresses predictive performance, longitudinal fairness, and explainability. Using the MIMIC-IV cohort, the LSTM achieves an AUC of 0.884 (95% CI: 0.859-0.908) on a held-out test set, comparable to contemporary tabular baselines (LightGBM 0.892, Random Forest 0.889, XGBoost 0.886, Logistic Regression 0.867) and substantially above a SOFA-only clinical baseline (0.770). Because three development-model predictors (vasopressors, mechanical ventilation, and the full SOFA score) are not consistently recorded in eICU, cross-institutional generalization is assessed with a common-feature Random Forest, yielding AUC 0.743 (95% CI: 0.738-0.749). We conduct a longitudinal simulation on the real MIMIC-IV cohort, with simulated performative feedback, across 15 retraining cycles and 16 intersectional subgroups, simultaneously monitoring TPR, FPR, and FOR gaps. Across 30 independent runs, all three strategies converge to final TPR gaps with no significant difference (Friedman $\chi ^{2}(2)=1.195$, $p=0.550$); however, the Dynamic Adaptive Fairness controller exhibits bounded, damped trajectories where static reweighing shows larger transient spikes. Under an auxiliary exogenous covariate shift, adaptive control attenuates the post-shift TPR-gap spike ($\Delta =+0.091$) relative to the no-intervention baseline ($\Delta =+0.139$). A cross-institutional eICU fairness audit reveals measurable per-hospital variability (TPR gap 0.134, FPR gap 0.060, FOR gap 0.032); subgroup estimates are reported with event counts and Wilson intervals. SHAP feature-importance rankings remain highly stable across cycles ($\rho =0.986$), anchored by clinical severity markers. The framework supports pre-deployment fairness stress testing and longitudinal governance of clinical AI.

paper.title: Large Language Models Predict Functional Outcomes After Acute Ischemic Stroke.
paper.abstract:
Background And Objectives: Accurate prediction of functional outcomes after acute ischemic stroke can guide clinical decision-making and resource allocation. Prior work has relied predominantly on structured predictors and conventional machine learning, while the ability of large language models (LLMs) to infer modified Rankin Scale (mRS) scores from routine clinical admission notes is largely unexplored.
Methods: We evaluated encoder (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers [BERT], NYUTron) and generative (Llama-3.1-8B, MedGemma-4B) LLMs, in both frozen and fine-tuned settings, for discharge and 90-day mRS prediction. ModernBERT-base was evaluated as a long-context encoder sensitivity analysis. We retrospectively analyzed 9485 admission history and physical notes for discharge prediction and 1898 notes for 90-day prediction from the NYU Langone Get With The Guidelines-Stroke registry (2016-2025). The most recent 12 months were held out for testing. Performance was assessed for binary functional outcome (mRS 0-2 vs 3-6) and compared with structured, hybrid, and clinical risk score baselines.
Results: In frozen settings, the clinically pretrained NYUTron encoder outperformed all other models. After fine-tuning, Llama achieved the highest discrimination for discharge (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve [AUROC] 0.84, area under the precision-recall curve 0.81) and 90-day (AUROC 0.87, area under the precision-recall curve 0.84) prediction, while binary accuracy was similar among NYUTron, Llama, and MedGemma. A long-context ModernBERT-base sensitivity analysis did not outperform NYUTron or eliminate differences in exact mRS prediction. For 90-day prediction, fine-tuned Llama outperformed structured (Zhang et al, AUROC 0.82), hybrid (Sung et al, AUROC 0.82), and clinical risk score (Totaled Health Risks in Vascular Events, AUROC 0.80; Stroke Prognostication using Age and NIH Stroke Scale, AUROC 0.79) baselines (all P < .05).
Conclusion: Fine-tuned LLMs can predict poststroke functional outcomes from admission notes alone and outperform the evaluated prognostic baselines. Task-specific adaptation altered relative model-class performance, with generative models achieving the strongest performance on several metrics; however, differences between model classes varied by metric and cannot be attributed to architecture alone. Our findings support the development of text-based prognostic tools that integrate into clinical workflows without manual data extraction.

paper.title: MVCNN model for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea prediction via facial photos.
paper.abstract:
Introduction: Polysomnography (PSG) is the gold standard for pediatric obstructive sleep apnea (OSA) diagnosis but is limited for large-scale screening and telemedicine by high costs and specialized requirements. Given the close correlation between craniofacial features and OSA, this study developed a non-invasive risk stratification model (non-OSA, mild OSA, and moderate-to-severe OSA) using two-dimensional multi-view facial photographs based on a Multi-View Convolutional Neural Network (MVCNN).
Materials And Methods: This multicenter retrospective study included 212 children with frontal and lateral facial photographs linked to polysomnography. Models were evaluated at the patient level after aggregating each participant's available image records. The MVCNN was internally evaluated in 149 patients and externally evaluated in 63 patients. Patient-level discrimination and classification metrics were estimated with bootstrap confidence intervals, and paired bootstrap analysis compared models evaluated on common patients.
Results: In the internal patient-level evaluation, MVCNN achieved a macro-AUC of 0.898 (95% CI, 0.863-0.930), macro-F1 of 0.839, balanced accuracy of 0.840, and overall accuracy of 0.846. Its macro-AUC exceeded those of ResNet-50 by 0.061 (95% CI, 0.022-0.106; P = 0.004) and VGG-16 by 0.104 (95% CI, 0.057-0.164; P < 0.001). In the external cohort, MVCNN achieved a macro-AUC of 0.876 (95% CI, 0.827-0.919), macro-F1 of 0.833, balanced accuracy of 0.826, and overall accuracy of 0.841.
Conclusions: Patient-level analyses support the discriminatory performance of multi-view facial photography for pediatric OSA risk stratification in the studied dental cohorts. Prospective validation, direct view-ablation studies, and calibration in broader clinical populations are required before clinical deployment.

paper.title: Development and validation of a deep learning model for predicting small-for-gestational-age birth using routine mid-trimester ultrasound.
paper.abstract:
Background: Small-for-gestational-age (SGA) birth is associated with increased perinatal morbidity and mortality. Earlier identification of pregnancies at risk could inform antenatal surveillance. We aimed to develop and externally test a deep learning model for predicting SGA birth using routine fetal ultrasound images acquired at 20-23 weeks of gestation.
Methods: This two-center retrospective study used case-enriched samples comprising 594 pregnancies (306 SGA; 2,970 images) at Center A and 407 pregnancies (164 SGA; 2,035 images) at Center B. SGA was defined as birth weight below the 10th percentile for gestational age and sex. Model development and five-fold cross-validation used Center A images, followed by evaluation on a held-out internal test set. Center B provided independent external testing without model updating. The model incorporated split-group convolution, channel attention, and multi-scale feature fusion. Performance was evaluated at the image level and compared with established deep learning architectures. Ablation analyses and gradient-weighted class activation mapping were also performed.
Results: Comparative and ablation experiments supported the contribution of the proposed modules. In the held-out internal image test set, the proposed model achieved an AUC of 0.8667, an F1-score of 0.8006, an MCC of 0.5820, and an accuracy of 0.7912. In the independent external image test set, it achieved an AUC of 0.8046, an F1-score of 0.7132, an MCC of 0.4845, and an accuracy of 0.7273.
Conclusions: The model showed image-level discrimination of subsequent SGA birth using routine mid-trimester ultrasound images in internal and independent external testing. Patient-level validation and assessment of calibration and clinical utility are needed before clinical implementation.

paper.title: Explainable volumetric deep learning from contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI for preoperative IDH prediction in adult-type diffuse gliomas: a two-center study.
paper.abstract:
Objective: To evaluate contrast-enhanced T1-weighted MRI (CE-T1WI) models for preoperative prediction of isocitrate dehydrogenase (IDH) mutation status in adult-type diffuse gliomas and explore phenotype associations of influential latent features.
Methods: This retrospective study included 462 patients. Center 1 provided training (n = 259) and internal-test (n = 65) cohorts, and Center 2 provided external validation (n = 138). Five input-architecture combinations and six classifiers were evaluated against an interpretable logistic benchmark combining age and Visually Accessible Rembrandt Images (VASARI) descriptors. For each architecture, the classifier with the highest observed external area under the curve (AUC) was selected for reporting. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, decision curves, and 100 downstream refits with fixed deep features. Shapley additive explanations (SHAP) and phenotype association analyses examined influential latent features and their relationships with clinical and imaging phenotypes.
Results: Region-of-interest (ROI)-constrained three-dimensional vision Transformer (3D ViT) with a support vector machine (SVM) achieved an external AUC of 0.929 (95% CI, 0.885-0.973), accuracy of 0.848, sensitivity of 0.838, specificity of 0.857, and Brier score of 0.106. The age-VASARI benchmark achieved an external AUC of 0.782. Across downstream refits, the ROI-constrained model had a mean external AUC of 0.930 and the smallest mean training-minus-external AUC difference (0.019). The same 10 features formed the highest-importance SHAP set across cohorts, with different rank orders. Feature_546 correlated with age (r = 0.461), postoperative Ki-67 (r = 0.562), and enhancement quality (r = 0.678; all adjusted p < 0.001).
Conclusion: ROI-constrained volumetric learning from CE-T1WI showed promising cross-center IDH discrimination using one routine MRI sequence. Influential latent features were associated with postoperative Ki-67 and recognizable imaging phenotypes. SHAP attribution and these exploratory associations provide complementary perspectives on model behavior in preoperative IDH assessment.

paper.title: A preliminary investigation into operationalizing machine learning for hip replacement outcomes: predicting OHS and EQ-5D VAS in Wales.
paper.abstract: Wales has an extensive program for collecting patient-reported outcome (PRO) measures data, and as a country with a population that generally views artificial intelligence use in healthcare positively, the development of machine learning (ML) models for patient outcome prediction offers an opportunity to advance value-based healthcare. This study discusses a preliminary case for the development of a predictive model for patients undergoing hip arthroplasty to assess challenges in creating such models in Wales, and the potential to support the training process with data from England. Five supervised ML models (logistic regression, extreme gradient boosting, elastic net, random forest, and neural net) were trained on data from England with a range of variables to predict postoperative hip replacement PROs based on predefined minimal clinically important difference thresholds for both generic (EQ-VAS) and condition-specific (Oxford Hip Score) PROs. The performance of the models on the English test set was similar across algorithms, with extreme gradient boosting achieving the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic for both PROs. Although the performance of the ML model dropped for both PROs when tested on Welsh data, the drop was more pronounced for the condition-specific Oxford Hip Score. Based on this case, four broad recommendations are presented for future ML model development for the National Health Service in Wales: standardization of the approach to missing data, preference for transparent ML methodologies, utilization of data linkage potential in Wales, and clinical agreement on metric prioritization.
